Saint Louis enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 28-5 overall and 15-3 in the Atlantic 10 after finishing first in the league and then losing 70-69 to Dayton in the A-10 tournament semifinals on March 14, 2026. ESPN’s schedule page lists the Billikens as the A-10 regular-season champion at 28-5, and Saint Louis’ official cumulative stats page confirms the full 33-game sample with 87.24 points scored per game and 69.52 allowed. The NCAA bracket pairing shown on ESPN has Saint Louis opening the NCAA Tournament against Georgia on Thursday, March 19, 2026. Saint Louis’ regular-season profile is built on volume efficiency: 50.9 percent from the field, 40.1 percent from three, 39.9 rebounds, and 18.3 assists per game, while holding opponents to 37.9 percent overall and 29.4 percent from three.

Offensively, this is a Josh Schertz team in the clearest possible sense: five-out spacing principles, a playmaking center hub in Robbie Avila, constant shooting gravity, and a willingness to play through handoffs, trail threes, quick extra passes, and spread pick-and-pop. The strongest evidence is statistical and game-specific. Avila leads the team in assists at 4.1 per game while also leading the team in scoring at 12.9, which tells you the offense is often initiated through him as a facilitator rather than through a traditional point guard. Saint Louis has 605 assists on 1,008 made field goals, an extremely high assisted-basket profile that matches Schertz’s long-documented preference for read-and-react, pass-heavy offense. In the 102-79 win over Saint Joseph’s on December 31, 2025, the Billikens assisted on 25 of 38 field goals and made a school-record 19 threes. In the 102-71 win over Dayton on January 30, 2026, they shot 17-of-28 from three and scored 25 fast-break points, showing that the scheme is not only half-court skill but also early-offense spacing after stops. In practical terms, the named actions that show up in results are Avila-centered pick-and-pop and dribble-handoff creation for Trey Green and Ishan Sharma, plus flare and relocation threes for wings. Green made 90 threes at 45.7 percent, Sharma made 77 at 42.8 percent, Avila made 62 at 41.6 percent, and Brady Dunlap made 45 at 44.1 percent. That four-man perimeter production is exactly what makes Schertz’s spacing and inside-out passing dangerous.

A traditional scout would call Saint Louis a “skill-over-force” offense, but not a soft one. Kellen Thames shoots 64.9 percent from the floor and gives them a downhill slasher/finisher who changes the geometry of the floor; Amari McCottry adds 10.3 points, 5.2 rebounds, and 2.8 assists as a secondary driver; Dion Brown scores 11.1 per game on a hyper-efficient 60.6 percent from the field as a cutter, dunker-spot finisher, and short-roll target. The best single-game proof of the offensive menu came in the March 4, 2026 win over Loyola Chicago: Saint Louis shot 60.4 percent overall, got 18 points from McCottry on 6-of-9 shooting, 15 from Brown on 6-of-6, and four assists from Avila. That is classic Schertz balance: touch passing from the 5, slot shooting, and slashers feeding off closeouts.

Defensively, Saint Louis is better than its reputation from Schertz’s earlier teams. The official numbers say opponents shot just 37.9 percent overall and 29.4 percent from three across 33 games. This is not a gambling pressure defense; it is more positional and coverage-based. The Bills average 7.2 steals and 3.5 blocks, so they can create events, but their identity is more about shrinking space, finishing possessions, and contesting the arc. The January 7, 2026 win at VCU is the cleanest schematic example: Saint Louis held VCU to 18-of-63 shooting, 6-of-24 from three, and 62 points. The February 13, 2026 win at Loyola Chicago was another: Saint Louis won 86-59 while limiting the Ramblers to 59 points. When locked in, they run shooters off the line and trust their positional size behind the play. Paul Otieno gives them rim protection depth at 0.8 blocks per game, Quentin Jones adds 0.8 blocks from the perimeter, and Thames leads the team in steals at 1.4 per game. The weak point is foul accumulation and physical matchups against power-driving teams; Brown averages 2.8 fouls, Jones 2.7, and McCottry 2.3, which can stress their rotations.

Schertz’s coaching philosophy is visible in the adjustment pattern. He wants offensive clarity, ball movement, and emotional poise, and when games wobble he usually adjusts through spacing and lineup rhythm rather than abandoning identity. The best documented example is the February 3, 2026 win at Davidson. Saint Louis trailed 46-41 at halftime, then, in the school recap’s own framing, “adjust[ed] in the second half” and won 91-82. Brady Dunlap hit all six of his threes and scored a career-high 22, which suggests Schertz found a way to free a weak-side shooter after the halftime reset. Another example came on March 4 against Loyola Chicago. After Loyola cut the margin to 62-54 with 8:36 left, Saint Louis answered with a 10-1 run with four different players scoring; that is a coach restoring order through execution rather than isolation. The negative example matters too: after the 86-57 loss at George Mason on March 7, a report quoted Schertz ripping both the offense and defense, which is useful scouting context because it shows he will publicly challenge effort when the team loses its discipline.

Late-game and clutch execution are mostly strong, though not flawless. On November 27, 2025, Saint Louis beat Santa Clara 71-70 when Kellen Thames drove and hit the game-winning basket in the final minute after Quentin Jones found him in the corner; SLU then got a stop on the last possession. On January 27, 2026, the Bills survived George Washington 79-76 in a one-possession conference game behind Trey Green’s 23 points. On January 20, they won 81-77 at Duquesne, a road grinder that showed they could close with free throws and half-court composure. But the warning games matter: they lost 81-76 at Rhode Island on February 17, lost 77-62 at Dayton on February 24, and then lost 70-69 to Dayton on March 14 in the A-10 tournament. That semifinal defeat is especially relevant because it was a one-point neutral-floor loss right before the NCAA Tournament; Saint Louis scored only 69 points with 18 turnovers, a bad number for an offense that usually plays clean.

The key players start with Avila. He is the offensive fulcrum: 12.9 points, 4.5 rebounds, 4.1 assists, 41.6 percent from three, and 80.5 percent from the line. His standout games include 23 points and seven assists against Duquesne on February 28, 22 points against George Washington in the A-10 tournament quarterfinal on March 13, and a 20-point, eight-assist game against Saint Joseph’s on December 31. Green is the top movement shooter and microwave scorer: 11.1 points per game, 90 made threes, 45.7 percent from deep. His signature stretch came in late January and early February, including 23 points against George Washington on January 27 and 23 more with seven made threes against Dayton on January 30. Sharma is the second elite spacer at 9.1 points per game and 77 made threes; he erupted for 29 points at St. Bonaventure on January 23. McCottry is the connective wing: 10.3 points, 5.2 rebounds, 2.8 assists, with 18 points against San Francisco on December 13 and 18 more against Loyola Chicago on March 4. Thames gives them force at the rim, shooting 64.9 percent and averaging 9.9 points; he had 24 in the February 24 loss at Dayton and 18 points, 10 rebounds, and three assists in the January 7 win at VCU. Brown is the efficient glue forward at 11.1 points on 60.6 percent shooting and 5.5 rebounds; he scored 21 against Purdue Fort Wayne on November 21 and had 15 on 6-of-6 shooting against Loyola Chicago on March 4.

The notable wins tell you what travels. Beating VCU 71-62 on the road on January 7 proved Saint Louis could defend a high-level A-10 opponent in a half-court game. The 102-79 destruction of Saint Joseph’s on December 31 showed ceiling offense against a quality league team, with 19 made threes. The 102-71 demolition of Dayton on January 30 showed how devastating the Billikens are when both Green and Sharma get loose off Avila-triggered creation. The 79-65 win over Loyola Chicago on March 4 clinched a share of the A-10 regular-season title and showed composure after Loyola made a push.

The notable losses reveal the upset formula. Stanford beat them 78-77 on November 28 in a one-possession neutral-floor game, showing Saint Louis can be vulnerable when the three-ball cools and the margin game gets tight. Rhode Island’s 81-76 win on February 17 showed a path through disruption; Saint Louis had 18 turnovers. Dayton’s 77-62 win on February 24 showed that if you make Saint Louis play through contact and take away rhythm threes, the offense can flatten. George Mason’s 86-57 blowout on March 7 is the red-flag tape: Saint Louis shot 39.7 percent overall and just 4-of-24 from three, which is the clearest proof that this team becomes ordinary when opponents win the physical battle and erase clean catch-and-shoot looks.

As for head coach Josh Schertz’s NCAA tournament history, this 2026 appearance with Saint Louis is his first NCAA Division I men’s tournament berth as a head coach. Saint Louis’ official bio states that his 2023-24 Indiana State team reached the NIT championship game after narrowly missing the NCAA field, so there is no Division I NCAA round history yet. However, the same official bio notes that at Lincoln Memorial he made 10 NCAA Division II tournaments and reached the 2016 Division II national championship game, which is equivalent to reaching the final round of that tournament level. So the short version for tournament experience is: no previous Division I NCAA tournament rounds reached as a head coach before 2026, but extensive Division II NCAA experience including the 2016 national title game.

Bottom line: Saint Louis is an elite shot-making, pass-first, modern offense with enough defensive structure to win two ways. The Billikens are at their best when Avila is orchestrating from the top or elbow, Green and Sharma are flying off movement into handoffs and pops, and Thames/McCottry are punishing closeouts. The vulnerability is clear too: physical opponents that switch or top-lock the shooting, force turnovers, and drag the game into a possession battle can make Saint Louis uncomfortable. If the game is played at Saint Louis’ pace and spacing, they look like a second-weekend offense. If it becomes a fistfight with 15-plus turnovers, the upset path is real.
